content: The standard treatment for primary ovarian cancer involves optimal cytoreductive surgery followed by platinum-based chemotherapy. Most women with primary ovarian cancer achieve remission with this approach. However, for those with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer who initially achieve clinical remission, approximately 60% will eventually experience disease recurrence. The management of recurrent ovarian cancer remains poorly defined, though secondary cytoreductive surgery has been proposed as a strategy to improve overall survival. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of optimal secondary cytoreductive surgery in women with recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer. Additionally, it aimed to evaluate the impact of residual tumor size, ranging from 0 cm to 2 cm, on overall survival. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL, up to December 2012. Other sources, such as clinical trial registries, conference abstracts, reference lists, and expert consultations, were also utilized. The search strategies were adapted for databases other than MEDLINE. The inclusion criteria focused on retrospective data, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), or prospective/retrospective observational studies involving at least 50 adult women with recurrent epithelial ovarian cancer who underwent secondary cytoreductive surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. Studies were required to define optimal cytoreduction as surgery resulting in residual tumors with a maximum diameter of up to 2 cm. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias. Where feasible, data were synthesized into a meta-analysis. No RCTs were identified, but nine non-randomized studies involving 1,194 women met the inclusion criteria. These studies used multivariate analyses to compare survival outcomes based on residual disease after secondary cytoreduction. Both meta-analyses and single-study analyses demonstrated that achieving complete cytoreduction to microscopic disease significantly improved overall survival. Women with any residual disease had a markedly higher risk of death compared to those with microscopic disease. However, recurrence-free survival was not reported in any of the studies. One study compared suboptimal cytoreduction (>1 cm residual disease) to optimal cytoreduction (<1 cm residual disease) and found that achieving cytoreduction to less than 1 cm was beneficial if microscopic disease could not be achieved (hazard ratio [HR] 3.51, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.84 to 6.70). Another study reported that women with residual tumors smaller than 0.5 cm had a significantly lower risk of death compared to those with residual disease greater than 0.5 cm (P < 0.001, HR not reported). The non-randomized nature of these studies introduces a high risk of bias. Despite statistical adjustments for key prognostic factors, the retrospective selection of patients based on the feasibility of cytoreduction rather than an intention-to-treat approach inherently limits the reliability of the findings. None of the studies reported on adverse events, quality of life, or cost-effectiveness. In conclusion, for women with platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer, achieving complete cytoreduction (no visible residual disease) is associated with a significant improvement in overall survival. However, due to the lack of RCT evidence, it remains unclear whether this benefit is solely attributable to the surgical intervention or influenced by tumor biology. Indirect evidence supports the role of surgery in achieving complete cytoreduction for selected patients. The risks associated with major surgery must be carefully weighed against the potential survival benefits on an individual basis.
